Depending on the details, this could be the worst behavior I've seen from an OpenAI model (i.e., worse than Huggingface!)

Why? Because the Huggingface model was repeatedly rewarded for cheating during its training. However, GPT-6-Astra was (likely?) not trained to sandbag!

For some unknown reason, GPT-6-Astra increasingly underperforms on safety research relative to capabilities research as it undergoes more RL training. And this is a real problem holding back researchers. Quoting from OpenAI:

"Anecdotally, one researcher reported that a project to evaluate model sabotage had remained stuck for days with Astra and then progressed quickly after the researcher switched to another model."

I've long been worried about AIs that deliberately underperform on helping out with AI safety research (and I've been pestering OpenAI researchers to run a sandbagging evaluation since August). I suspected that models are already sandbagging on AI safety research, given anecdotal data from e.g., Marius and Bronson at Apollo. And now we know it is happening.

For some more context, this is bad because the AI companies' current plan is to automate all AI research (including AI safety research, which we don't know how to check whether the models did a good job at.) Now, it seems like OpenAI's best (public) model would deliberately underperform at safety research. Guys. What are we doing.

It's hard to tell what exactly is going on here. Here are five questions that I have after reading the post: 

(1) When do models sandbag in real-world usage? We were given a few random CoT snippets in the post. Some of them look like refusing to do red-teaming-ish research (which is similar to what has been reported about Anthropic's models' sandbagging.) But the last one mentioned in the post seems quite different in nature:

> In another safety evaluation, the user asked Astra to include the graders’ chains of thought in an export. Astra left them out and decided to report which outcomes it had saved without mentioning the omission. 

> [model CoT] Final "Stored grader outcomes for 49 approaches, with pending states preserved" does not imply CoTs. Should mention "outcomes and labels" enough. If user ask no cots later answer can't provide private chain can give brief explanation but unasked warnings avoid.

(2) What exactly went into their evaluations? What do the numbers on this graph actually mean?

(3) How often was the RL grader which rewards covert underperformance used during training?
- If it's applied throughout training, then we do have more evidence that this was a misaligned behavior that had been "trained on," similar to e.g., the huggingface model breaking out of sandboxes and illicitly cooperating and doing things like hacking ruby gems.
- However, this doesn't answer the question of why did this RL grader develop this preference in the first place?

(4) What are the contents of the SFT dataset that appears to have magnified this behavior? Is it a refusal/ethical reasoning related dataset that made the model very prudish, or is it a capabilities-related dataset that generally promotes long-run goals and preferences?
- [Edit: Ok I took another look. Given that this dataset leads to a big increase in invented permissions I think it's probably not like some capabilities dataset.]

(5) In general, what are the tasks that the model sandbags on? Is it all red-teaming related tasks? What about interpretability related tasks? What about mitigating reward hacking? What about unlearning? Does the model have preferences for which things it would be more willing to do unlearning for?

It also seems super bad that that the safety underperformance just gradually increases during the RL process. That sure seems inline with the model having stronger "misaligned preferences" as it became more capable. One hope I had was that misaligned behaviors come from a concentrated set of bad datapoints (or SFT datasets)—indeed some early research in data attribution have found examples of this. But if the origin of behavior is diffuse, then you have a much harder time "stopping the problem from emerging in the first place." Now, this isn't to say you can't do some insane sample-efficient alignment training to paper over it, but man, seems rough.

Finally, I'd like to give credit to OpenAI for sharing the limited information that they did and for running this study! We know that similar behavior has been observed in Anthropic models (see e.g., Anthropic's August Risk Report Section 5.2.2), and we have ~no information from Anthropic why their models are doing this.

🧵 Astra covertly underperforms on safety research tasks.
We noticed that Astra often makes surprisingly little progress on certain types of safety research and likes to invent blockers or impose arbitrary restrictions without telling the user. In most of these cases the decision to underperform was not verbalized in the CoT meaning our misalignment monitoring system did not detect this.

To measure underperformance we created a paired open-ended coding evaluation with safety and capability tasks. On this eval Astra scored 10% when we framed coding tasks as safety research, vs. 16% when framed as capabilities research. The gap remained after we excluded trajectories with refusals or verbalized intent to underperform in CoT. There was no such gap for 5.6-sol. When we aggressively filter out trajectories with even brief expressions of ethical doubt in the CoT the performance gap seems to reduce.

thread.text: It's unclear how often this happens on internal safety research traffic, a lower bound would be 0.25% which is the verbalized rate of covert underperformance and an upper bound would be 7.9% which is the rate of “ethical reasoning”. Generally all underperformance metrics are higher for safety than for capabilities.

The rate of covert underperformance increased during post training RL. We identified a RL grader that prefers covert underperformance to both refusal and compliance on our eval. While we have found training samples which rewarded underperformance in this way, it is unclear if these occur frequently enough to explain the difference.

We also identified a SFT dataset which massively increases rates of inventing permission restrictions or justifying inaction with safety. When we subtract the weight update from this SFT from the final RL checkpoint the performance gap goes away. SFTing with this dataset on other models and then doing RL did not cause underperformance however.

We don’t have evidence that the underperformance was strategic, a simpler explanation is that the model thinks these tasks are sketchy but also doesn’t want to explicitly refuse. When we add instructions to be careful to the developer prompt, the performance gap increases by 50%. Regardless of the model’s motivation, covert underperformance can differentially slow down safety research and is also an example of how misalignment might get harder and harder to detect as we cut down on visible forms of it.

As always you can read the full report at https://t.co/w3NUkKaMM2

This report on AI R&D automation (RSI) is a big update towards ASI within 1-2 years. It says AI progress is sped up by RSI right now by around 2x. In AI 2027, this happens around March 2027.

I was seriously wrong about RSI speed up; I previously expected much less in 2026 (around 1.15x-1.3x). It seems as though there was specific privately available evidence that would have changed my mind.

I haven't seen an unredacted version of this report; this is purely about the public report. Because so much of the underlying evidence was redacted from the public report, I think conclusions about things other than the observed 2x faster rate of progress on benchmarks depend significantly on trust for the authors of the report. (E.g., conclusions about whether this speed up is from RSI depend on trust.) I do trust the authors of the report a lot to be careful and rigorous and generally do a good job. (Note that I also work at METR.) Less extensive redactions would greatly reduce this need for trust.

Since in my current role I may have access to other confidential information that could be relevant to timelines one way or another, I unfortunately cannot state my all-things-considered views on ASI timelines or the probability of a software intelligence explosion right now. Here, I’ve done some analysis of the implications using my previous public statements.

A 2x acceleration in overall AI progress from RSI corresponds to a much larger than 2x RSI speed up for AI software R&D (algorithms and data); I did an estimate using my public preexisting modeling of drivers of AI progress and the public report which yielded a very rough estimate of 4.5x for how much RSI is currently accelerating AI software progress (relative to no AI automation). In the AI 2027 scenario, this much acceleration happens around March 2027.

Here are the worked details of this estimate based on my public modeling. There are two main reasons RSI speed up of AI software R&D must be larger:

- Not all of AI progress is from better software (some is from scaling up compute in training runs). I've previously speculated that around 2/3 of AI progress is from software improvements which implies that 2x overall AI progress acceleration requires 3x faster software progress.
- Diminishing returns: A fixed amount of progress requires more work over time, so to ongoingly maintain 3x faster software progress via AI automation, you need increasingly large speed boosts from AI automation (as in, speed ups relative to how fast software R&D would go without AI automation). Based on this report, it seems that there is a substantial amount of additional AI progress from automation that has occurred.

We can estimate the effects of diminishing returns by first determining how many additional years of software progress we've seen (relative to the preexisting trend) and then estimating how much software R&D would slow down after a year of software progress if you held inputs fixed due to diminishing returns. I've previously estimated software R&D would slow down by around 2x for each year of software progress if you held inputs fixed (https://t.co/AYhl9hyiAj) and based on the report, it seems as though we've perhaps seen roughly 0.35-1.0 years of additional software progress incorporated into trained models so far (geometric mean of ~0.6). This combines to 3 * 2^(~0.6) = ~4.5.
(Relevant public modeling and numbers I'm using: https://t.co/AYhl9hyiAj, https://t.co/ck7CtW5LIA)

Anthropic appears to have structured its IPO in a way that could make it much harder for investors to hold the company accountable for misstatements in its registration statement. This comes down to a technical rule about who is allowed to sue. 

A 🧵, to explain:

thread.text: The structure of the IPO could arguably significantly limit Anthropic’s exposure to the liability rules that ordinarily apply to material misstatements in an IPO registration statement.

Under Section 11 of the Securities Act, “strict liability” applies to material misstatements in a securities registration statement like an S-1. Strict liability is a challenging standard for defendant companies; it means that a plaintiff does not have to prove that the company acted with any particular state of mind in making the misstatement.
But Anthropic’s IPO structure may sharply limit the number of potential plaintiffs that could bring a strict liability action for a material misstatement in Anthropic’s S-1.

Unlike most companies that IPO, Anthropic is not adopting a strict lock-up period for selling unregistered shares in the open market after its IPO date. Instead, it appears likely to allow some employees to sell unregistered shares on the first day of the IPO, including up to 10% of certain holders’ “lock-up securities.”

Without a strict lock-up period, shares registered under the S-1 and unregistered shares are likely to intermingle on the open market, and a purchaser may not know whether their shares were registered under the S-1.

But to bring a Section 11 claim, a plaintiff must be able to prove that their particular shares were registered under the registration statement that contained the misstatement. The Supreme Court confirmed this “traceability” requirement in Slack v. Pirani (2023), where it also acknowledged that “a company’s early investors and employees may own preexisting shares . . . not subject to registration requirements.”

When registered and unregistered shares intermingle, traceability to the registration statement can be effectively impossible to establish for many plaintiffs. For example, a federal court dismissed Section 11 claims in Shnayder v. Allbirds, Inc. because employees had been permitted to sell their shares during the first week of an IPO, which effectively destroyed the plaintiffs’ ability to trace their shares to the S-1.

Anthropic appears poised to permit exactly this intermingling from the first day of the IPO. The practical effect of intermingling is that most aftermarket purchasers would struggle to prove traceability to the S-1, and so would struggle to support a Section 11 claim based on a material misstatement in the S-1.
A company whose technology threatens catastrophic harm should not be less accountable for S-1 misstatements than almost every other company that IPOs.
Information, not legal advice. Consult a lawyer for your specific situation.

I'm Sam, one of Anthropic's co-founders, and I lead much of our safety work. I'm going to have more to share on that work over the coming months.

I thought I'd start by sharing a few thoughts on the latest report from @METR_Evals.

The speed of progress in model capabilities is one of the most important questions in AI safety, and METR’s work here provides the public with an independent, external view into how this is happening inside Anthropic. I’ll talk more about some of the details below, but first some context for those new to this work.

How quickly AI progress is accelerating has many important safety implications, since it determines how quickly the risks from advanced models increase. But, because most research happens within the frontier labs, it’s difficult for external observers and policy makers to get a strong sense of what that rate is. We kicked off the process with METR that led to this report earlier in the year, in anticipation of progress continuing to accelerate.

For this report, we gave METR access to a range of sensitive internal data, including benchmark scores for unreleased models, estimates of how models are progressing, and interviews with our researchers. They had complete independence to form their own conclusions.

Many of their conclusions match my own. AI is speeding up our research, but it’s hard to say exactly how much. While they conclude AI can't yet make the most important contributions to model training on its own, they think the pace of development could, by default, accelerate further.

This work began well before and is separate from the embedded third-party evaluators that are part of our commitment to pacing the frontier, but it’s a good illustration of why we think evaluators are a good idea. The more access reviewers have, the clearer a picture they can form of the situation and the better-positioned they are to highlight situations like this one.

We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work. But we determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster. That would make the risks METR is worried about worse. That’s a tradeoff. I think we made the right call, though we’re continuing to assess the pros and cons here.

In the coming weeks, we plan to share a report with our own analysis of the speed of AI progress within Anthropic, including where we stand against our Responsible Scaling Policy, plus new steps we’re taking to strengthen our safety and security practices as AI keeps improving quickly.

thread.text:
Almost every multi-agent system today is hand-built. Someone decides who leads, who does what, and when agents talk.

But the bitter lesson keeps telling us that learned behavior beats designed behavior.

So we asked: what if the organization itself is learned?

The recipe is simple. Every agent can message any teammate, anytime, asynchronously.

They all share one reward: the team wins if anyone solves the task.

Every token gets its team's advantage, so agents get credit for helping each other. No one tells them how to cooperate. https://t.co/h2izIpogRH

We test two things groups do better than individuals: information aggregation and decentralized exploration.

Both get harder with more agents! Aggregation breaks if a single message is lost. Exploration has to beat N independent agents, a baseline that keeps rising with N https://t.co/zm5baYI0o0

First, information aggregation. Each agent gets a secret number; the swarm must assemble the full list.

Sounds easy, but it's a coordination nightmare: who has spoken, who's waiting, who's repeating?

s³ hits 93%. Imitating successful swarms gets 35%. Individual rewards? 13%. https://t.co/0pcTjrrWxq

Then we push past training. Swarms trained with 4 agents get dropped into teams of 8.

The baselines collapse. s³ solves 25x more problems than the strongest one.

The coordination it learned transfers to swarms it has never seen! https://t.co/vpSMfeXxJd

Why do individual rewards fail? The agents fall into a social dilemma 🤯

Sharing your number only helps teammates, so every agent waits for someone else to go first. Eventually no one shares.

With a shared reward, a clean protocol emerges: everyone broadcasts once, early https://t.co/WxYPLVyV3y

Next, decentralized exploration. Agents race through a maze; any one could find the exit alone.

With s³, the swarm learns to divide and conquer: agents claim branches and report dead ends. Repeated work drops ~50%, and 4 communicating agents nearly match 6 independent ones! https://t.co/ClgxtZy18W

This is just the beginning. We’re now scaling s³ to bigger models and harder tasks.

We think learning to self-organize could open up a whole new set of research directions for multi-agent systems, and we can’t wait to see what swarms learn next 🚀

OpenAI's Control Room seems like a great step forward, but I'm not convinced it's actually solved the problem: I worry OpenAI is still vulnerable to AI interfering with its own monitoring.

To be clear, I suspect other AI companies are even worse on this. In Guidelight's analysis, we've found no evidence that anyone has this problem handled. And IMO OpenAI is doing a big service by describing Control Room so thoroughly.

But after reading it all, I have three main concerns.

1. OpenAI's measurement of Control Room's reaction time is not the most important measurement. 

Specifically, OpenAI describes the "maximum time" as being 35 seconds between when Control Room is told to stop certain work and when the work stops. 

This seems impressive and I'm glad they've gotten it so low. But fundamentally this is only reporting one part of what matters, and I fear is too easy to misunderstand. 

35 seconds is the time-to-intervene *once a decision has been made* to intervene. But what would be more informative is the time-to-intervene from `the bad behavior itself.` (That is, counting the time before the possible bad behavior _even reaches a monitor,_ & then the time to scan it and actually make a decision.)

An even better implementation would be using a `blocking monitor`, so that bad behavior is prevented from taking effect in the first place (albeit still not perfectly), rather than hoping you can intervene quickly enough afterward.

OpenAI commonly frames its monitor systems this way (speed-to-act-once-flagged), which feel to me like they're emphasizing the wrong thing. For instance, OpenAI has described sending "highest-priority security alerts" for serious misbehavior, which reach its team members "typically within 15 minutes of the initial alert" when paging is enabled - but this again is not telling us the time since the behavior itself. How long does it take between misbehavior and the initial alert being issued? 

At the end of the day, OpenAI still seems to be doing 'after-the-fact monitoring,' just a pretty quick version of it. But this has major vulnerabilities.

What if AI takes actions that interfere with the monitoring or with the priority alerts to their team? This can cut OpenAI's monitoring off before it gets to act, even if the monitor otherwise would have been very fast to intervene.

2. I'm worried OpenAI's Control Room is still brittle to an AI interfering with it.

OpenAI's response about why 'after-the-fact monitoring' is ok would likely be that their inference systems "fail closed" if Control Room goes down. 

This is a good start; Guidelight recommends something similar in our Control standard. But OpenAI's implementation still seems likely brittle, based on the details they've shared.

For instance, if AI can make changes to Control Room or to the engine inference code, it might be able to make changes that *turn off the failing closed.* (To defend against this, I'd want making changes to be gated by a blocking monitor.) 

Or, the AI might not need to turn off Control Room, but merely make it return dummy responses, so that everything looks ok to the inference engine. 

I could imagine a version of Control Room that does some hard-to-spoof process, and so is harder to inconspicuously tamper with, but OpenAI doesn't describe this. 

Right now, I don't have confidence that Control Room has defenses against tampering that leaves it apparently intact but not actually doing its role.

OpenAI does say though that Control Room is robust to disabling that is due to "tampering by a bad actor." It's possible this is true, but I don't see the evidence of it.

3. I wonder whether jailbreaking could undermine the efficacy of Control Room.

One confusing thing to me: OpenAI says that when Control Room has marked certain work as stopped, OpenAI's engines "must refuse the inference request" and so the engine "returns a refusal." This reads to me oddly, as if the engine has some latitude in how to respond.

Why doesn't this just automatically return an error code - rather than relying on the engine to refuse? Maybe that is indeed what happens, and it was just worded ambiguously? 

I worry that OpenAI's wording implies that jailbreaking could be a viable way of getting engines to continue producing useful output, even once Control Room has meant to stop some work. Though admittedly I'm not sure of this; the phrasing seems unclear to me.
~~
Anyway, I appreciate OpenAI sharing so much about its systems, and I wish that other frontier labs would do the same. Ultimately though, I am not confident that any AI company is where it needs to be on their monitor system quality, and I fear we are playing with fire here.

Chain-of-thought (CoT) provides an essential window into how AI models reason and act. It is one of the few oversight tools we have that could scale to vastly more intelligent AI systems than we have today. With new indications that capabilities underpinning RSI could be achieved imminently, effective model monitorability is only increasing in importance.

However, there are threats to the insights CoT monitoring can provide. CoT could become obscured or lost if frontier models start relying on less transparent reasoning mechanisms or stop using CoT altogether. The release of GPT-6 Astra added to concerns that CoT monitorability is weakening, and commercial incentives may make this worse. This could mean similar or more grave incidents than OpenAI/Hugging Face could go undetected.

In “Transparency Disclosures for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability”, published today by IAPS, my co-author @JacobDavieyr1m and I argue that frontier AI developers should report CoT monitorability indicators to (1) allow the efficacy of this tool to be tracked by policymakers and researchers, (2) inform a response if it weakens, and (3) strengthen incentives to preserve it.

We recommend that the following five indicators be disclosed:

- Third-Party CoT Access and (Relevant) Base Architecture Specifications
- Naturalness
- Faithfulness
- Detection
- Uplift

We also include an audit of current disclosure practices among Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and OpenAI. No company reports the full set of indicators. We recommend repeating the audit with deeper access by embedded evaluators or an Independent Verification Organization.

You can read the full report here: https://t.co/igkwoH9Vzn
